1.f4.name: Bird's Opening
1.f4.background: Named after Henry Bird, the English master who first played it in 1855 and kept playing it for forty years; the Hereford Times coined the name in 1885. It is a Dutch Defence with colours reversed.

1.f4 d5.name: Bird's Opening: Dutch Variation
1.f4 d5.strategy: The main reply: Black takes a stake in the centre and controls e4, so White's natural e-pawn advance is not available for free. The game becomes a mirror image of a Dutch set-up, with White's extra tempo against Black's solid structure.

1.f4 Nf6.strategy: A flexible developing move: the knight controls e4, so White cannot easily claim the centre with a pawn there, and Black keeps every set-up open. Most games settle into the same quiet structures as after 1...d5, with Black deciding how to meet White's plan later.

1.f4 f5.strategy: Mirrors White and takes e4 under control with a pawn, but Black opens the e8-h5 diagonal around their own king just as White did. Sound and quiet if White plays patiently, while a central pawn sacrifice can make the game sharp at once.

1.f4 e5.name: Bird's Opening: From's Gambit
1.f4 e5.background: Named after the Danish player Martin Severin From (1828–1895). It is popular at club level, where amateurs know less about it and there are many traps.
1.f4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to exploit the e1-h4 diagonal that 1.f4 has opened, then goes after the exposed king. Sharp but risky: if White accepts and plays carefully, Black has to pay for the pawn, and White can also sidestep the gambit by transposing to a King's Gambit.

1.f4 h6.strategy: Prepares ...g5 so that the advance is backed by a pawn instead of being a pure sacrifice. But it spends a move on the edge and weakens the kingside, and White builds a broad centre at leisure.

1.f4 Nh6.name: Bird's Opening: Horsefly Defence
1.f4 Nh6.background: The move is attributed to Martin Appleberry.
1.f4 Nh6.strategy: An odd-looking knight that eyes g4 and f5, and is safe on the rim because White's d2 pawn blocks the c1-bishop's diagonal. It avoids weakening any pawn and keeps the centre options open, but the knight is far from the action and needs time to find a better square.

1.f4 b5.name: Bird's Opening: Myers Defence
1.f4 b5.strategy: An offbeat flank advance that takes queenside space and prepares the c8-bishop for the long diagonal, where it presses on e4. White can occupy the centre, but then has trouble defending e4 while also going after the advanced b-pawn.

1.f4 g5.name: Bird's Opening: Hobbs Gambit
1.f4 g5.strategy: Throws a pawn forward to open lines against White's kingside, but White simply takes it, or hands it back at the right moment and leaves Black with a loosened kingside and nothing to show for the time spent.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight covers e5 and h4, so ...Qh4+ is no longer a worry, and it blocks no pawn. White keeps the choice between a kingside fianchetto, a compact pawn wall or a build-up for the e4 break for later.

1.f4 d5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares to put the c1-bishop on the long diagonal, where together with the f-pawn it gives White a double hold on e5. A quiet, flexible set-up that delays the knight's development, so Black has time to develop actively.

1.f4 d5 2.c4.name: Bird's Opening: Sturm Gambit
1.f4 d5 2.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once and offers the c-pawn, but it is not a real gambit: Black who clings to the extra pawn gets into difficulties through White's quick development, and the best reply is to strike back in the centre with 2...d4.

1.f4 d5 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for the centre and open lines, but Black takes it with 2...dxe4 and keeps it. White's weakened kingside leaves little to attack with, so the pawn is hard to win back and the gambit does not pay.

1.f4 d5 2.g4.name: Bird's Opening: Dutch Variation, Dudweiler Gambit
1.f4 d5 2.g4.strategy: Gives away a pawn for nothing and tears open the kingside: 2...Bxg4 takes it at once, and 2...e5 threatens ...Qh4 mate along the diagonal White has just opened, so White has to spend time on defence.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops, backs up d5 and keeps e4 under control, so White's plan of an e4 break meets a ready answer. Black mirrors White's development, stays solid and waits for White to declare which set-up it is playing for.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, so that it bears down the long diagonal while the pawns in front of the king stay compact. Black keeps the centre flexible and sets up solidly, leaving it to White to decide how sharp the game becomes.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Takes d4 away from White and claims queenside space, but develops nothing. White can finish development undisturbed and aim for the e4 break, so Black has gained room at the cost of time.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and builds a compact chain with f4 and e3 behind a future pawn on d4, a solid plan aimed at a later kingside attack. The price is the c1-bishop, which is shut in behind e3 until White finds it a diagonal.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle quickly. The pawn on g3 also closes the e1-h4 diagonal, which is the weak point of the f4 set-up, and the bishop will press on the long diagonal while White aims for an e4 break later.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop so that it, the f4 pawn and the knight on f3 all bear on e5. White fights for the dark squares and keeps the choice of where to put the king's bishop and the other knight open.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 c5.name: Bird's Opening: Lasker Variation
1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before White can set up the pawn chain, so the planned centre is challenged at once. Black gets active, open play instead of a quiet mirrored game, but gives up the option of backing d5 with a pawn.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to the long diagonal and castle early, a compact set-up that keeps the pawns around the king where they are. Black mirrors White's slow build-up and stays flexible about the centre.

1.f4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6.strategy: Backs d5 with a pawn and frees the king's bishop, a solid set-up. The price is the c8-bishop, which is shut in behind the pawn chain, and a passive game in which White builds its slow plan without much to disturb it.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5.strategy: Accepts the gambit and wins the pawn, the soundest answer. The cost is a weakened kingside: the e1-h4 diagonal is open and Black has ...Qh4+ available at once, so White has to play accurately and keep the king covered.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3.name: Bird's Opening: From's Gambit, Bahr Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.Nc3.strategy: Declines the pawn and develops, planning e4 for a broad centre. But Black simply takes on f4 and keeps the extra pawn, so White has given up a pawn without having won one. Taking the gambit is the better way to meet it.

1.f4 e5 2.d4.strategy: Ignores the attack on f4 and seizes space, offering a pawn for the initiative. Black can simply take and keep the extra pawn on a healthy structure, while White's king is still exposed on the e1-h4 diagonal.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn and removes White's central pawn, with the queen's route to h4 already open. Black keeps the extra pawn for now, and White must show that the open lines are worth it.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exf4.strategy: Takes the other pawn, but nothing defends it: the c1-bishop recaptures at once and White is left with the pawn on d4 and a free hand in the centre. Black has won no material and White is better developed.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the centre, but leaves e5 hanging: either capture on e5 wins a pawn and hits the knight with a pawn, and Black has only quick play against White's loosened kingside to show for it.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3.strategy: Attacks the pawn on d4 and covers h4, so Black's queen check disappears. White offers the pawn only for the moment: Black has to find a way to keep it.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once and centralises the queen. It comes out early, though: ...Nc6 attacks it with a developing move, so White loses time and Black has the better development.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to open the position for the pieces: if Black takes it, White is two pawns down with only a lead in development to show.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Holds the extra pawn by defending d4 with a pawn and takes space on the queenside. Black avoids having to give material back at once, though development is still behind White's.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with an attack on d4 and keeps the game simple. It does not hold the pawn, though: White takes back on d4 and, after the trade of knights, regains the pawn, leaving an even game with Black's king's knight still to come out.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and watches e4, but leaves d4 undefended: White simply takes it back with the knight, which stands well in the centre, and Black's extra pawn is gone.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5 4.c3.name: Bird's Opening: Siegener Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5 4.c3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to rip the centre open: if Black takes, Nxc3 brings a piece out into open lines. White is already a pawn down and has to make the initiative count, so it is a gambit that demands accurate follow-up.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5 4.e3.strategy: Attacks d4 a second time with a pawn and opens the lines of both bishops. If Black takes, White recovers a pawn with a tempo-gaining bishop development, and if Black holds on, the exchange on d4 gives White an open game. White needs fast development to justify the pawn.

1.f4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 c5 4.Nxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn but cannot keep the knight: ...cxd4 wins it for a pawn, and the queen's recapture on d4 leaves White a knight down for a pawn.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6.strategy: Challenges the pawn on e5 at once and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal towards White's kingside. Black accepts a pawn deficit for quick development and an initiative against the exposed king, the soundest way to play the gambit.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 Nc6.name: Bird's Opening: Schlechter Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 Nc6.strategy: Hits the pawn on e5 with a developing move, a calmer try that keeps the queen's diagonal open. It is obscure and not very dangerous: Black regains the pawn, but White drives the knight back with a central pawn and builds a broad centre, while careless development lets ...g5 give Black a good game.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 f6.name: Bird's Opening: Lasker Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 f6.strategy: Attacks e5 with a pawn, but it blocks the queen's own route to h4, and after the exchange on f6 Black is still a pawn down with an airy king and no compensation for it.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 Ne7.name: Bird's Opening: Platz Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 Ne7.strategy: The knight blocks the d8-h4 diagonal that the whole gambit relies on, and heads for g6 to attack e5. It is slow, and White uses the time to consolidate the extra pawn.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6.strategy: Wins a second pawn and plants a pawn on d6 that attacks c7 and e7 and cramps Black's position. Black must recapture quickly, while White has to keep the open e1-h4 diagonal in mind.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and covers h4 at once, so the ...Qh4+ tricks of the main line never arise. If Black retakes on e5, the knight takes that pawn too and White is still a pawn up, with the f-file half open for later.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and meets ...dxe5 with dxe5, keeping the extra pawn. It allows Black to trade queens, which costs White the right to castle, and the pawn on e5 needs defending against ...Nc6.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6.strategy: Recovers a pawn with a developing move that opens the b8-h2 diagonal and threatens ...Qh4+. Black is still a pawn down but has the initiative, and a careless reply loses at once: after 4.Nc3?? Qh4+ and a queen sacrifice on g3 mate.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Nf6.name: Bird's Opening: From's Gambit, Langheld Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Nf6.strategy: Develops instead of recapturing, but 4.dxc7 then attacks the queen and, after ...Qxc7, leaves Black two pawns down. The bishop recapture on d6 is the way to get the pawn back.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Qxd6.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which looks along the open diagonal at g3 and h2. Black is still a pawn down and has developed no piece, so White can bring out pieces and cover the kingside in peace.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3.strategy: The best move: the knight develops and covers h4, taking the sting out of ...Qh4+. Anything careless, such as 4.Nc3??, runs into ...Qh4+ and a queen sacrifice on g3 that mates. White keeps the extra pawn.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.g3.strategy: Closes the e1-h4 diagonal with a pawn so that ...Qh4+ cannot come, but the pawn is attacked by the bishop on d6 and must stay defended. White keeps the extra pawn, but the move develops nothing and loosens the light squares around the king.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops, but walks into the very trap the f-pawn's absence invites: ...Qh4+ forces g3, and the queen sacrifice ...Qxg3+ hxg3 Bxg3 is mate.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 g5.name: Bird's Opening: From's Gambit, Lasker Variation
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 g5.background: Emanuel Lasker, the future world champion, introduced 4...g5 in the game Bird–Lasker at Newcastle upon Tyne in 1892. It is the most common and most aggressive reply to 4.Nf3.
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 g5.strategy: The most aggressive try: the pawn aims to drive the knight from f3 and so reopen the h4 square. But Black is already a pawn down, the advance loosens the king's cover, and White steadies the position and heads for an ending where the extra pawn counts.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Develops towards g4 and f5 without moving a pawn, so the king's cover stays intact. The knight lands on the rim, though, and loses time, while White keeps the extra pawn and a free hand in the centre.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and aims it at g4 and h2, so Black builds pressure on the weakened kingside without loosening its own pawns. White has the extra pawn, but must keep the kingside covered, and Black has the active pieces.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops towards the centre and leaves the kingside pawns alone, a quieter plan than an attack on the king. Black aims at e5 and d4 and tries to make the pieces count against White's extra pawn.

1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 Nh6.name: Bird's Opening: From's Gambit, Lipke Variation
1.f4 e5 2.fxe5 d6 3.exd6 Bxd6 4.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Claims the centre and in the same stroke opens the c1-bishop's diagonal: the bishop now attacks the knight on h6, and Bxh6 would double Black's pawns. White keeps the extra pawn with a healthy centre.

Opens the f1-bishop for quick development and castling while the knight stays on f3 to guard h4 and h2. The c1-bishop is shut in behind the pawn, which is the price of the solid set-up; White keeps the extra pawn.

Develops a piece towards the centre, but loses time over it while Black's pieces aim at the kingside: a knight on g4 would attack h2 together with the bishop on d6, so White must keep h2 defended. The c1-bishop remains shut in.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 exf4.strategy: Takes the pawn and keeps it: White has declined the gambit but never won a pawn back, so Black is simply a pawn up. Black has to meet the coming central advance with care, but the extra pawn is a lasting asset.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops and covers e5, so that a capture there is answered by ...Nxe5 and the pawns stay level. It declines the extra pawn, and White keeps the freedom to choose the centre.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, a solid reply. It leaves the pawn on f4 alone, so Black gives up the chance to be a pawn up and White keeps a free hand in the centre.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 exf4 3.e4.name: Dunst Opening: Nowokunski Gambit
1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 exf4 3.e4.strategy: Plays without the f-pawn for a broad centre and quick development, and leaves Black to prove the extra pawn can be kept. The price is the king: the e1-h4 diagonal is open, and ...Qh4+ comes at once, so White has to spend time on the king while still a pawn down.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 exf4 3.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move, and it answers the problem of the position: the knight covers h4, so ...Qh4+ down the open diagonal no longer comes with tempo. White builds a centre and develops quickly, while Black has to prove that the extra pawn on f4 can be kept without loosening the kingside.

1.f4 e5 2.Nc3 exf4 3.g3.strategy: Shuts the e1-h4 diagonal and invites ...fxg3, after which hxg3 gives the rook the h-file and White some open lines for the pieces. White is still a pawn down and the kingside is thinned out, so it needs quick development to make up for it.

1.f4 f5 2.d4.strategy: Answers the symmetry with a calm central pawn: d4 joins f4 in holding e5 and frees the queen's bishop, so White can build a compact wall of pawns. It is solid and low-risk, but Black can mirror the set-up, and the game stays closed and level rather than sharp.

1.f4 f5 2.e4.name: Bird's Opening: Wagner-Zwitersch Gambit
1.f4 f5 2.e4.strategy: Offers a pawn to pull Black's f-pawn away from the king and open the e8-h5 diagonal, gambling that quick development is worth the material. It is a real try, but if Black keeps calm and takes, White has only the initiative to show for the pawn.

1.f4 f5 2.b3.strategy: The quiet, flexible reply: the queen's bishop is aimed down the long diagonal and White commits nothing in the centre. Black can copy the set-up, but White keeps a slightly freer game and the better pawn structure.

1.f4 f5 2.Nf3.strategy: A developing move that controls e5 and d4 and keeps the choice of set-up open, most often a fianchetto of the king's bishop and early castling. It is solid and level, a game of manoeuvring rather than an attack on the king.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn and keeps it, leaving a pawn on e4 that cramps White. The cost is the open e8-h5 diagonal in front of Black's king and a lag in development, so Black has to bring the pieces out carefully and be ready to give the pawn back if needed.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 d6.strategy: Declines the pawn: if White takes on f5, the bishop recaptures with a developing move and material is level. Black gets a solid game, but gives up the extra pawn that taking on e4 would keep and leaves White a free hand in the centre.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 e5.strategy: A counter-gambit that does not work: White takes on f5 and threatens Qh5+, because the f-pawn has left Black's king without cover on that diagonal. Black can win back the f4 pawn, but the king stays exposed and White gets the initiative.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops with tempo by attacking the pawn on e4, so Black must spend a move defending it. This is the more ambitious way to chase the pawn: White wants quick piece play and open lines instead of a slow build-up, and accepts that the pawn is not yet won back.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.d3.strategy: The main line: White gives a second pawn to open the position, and after ...exd3 the bishop recaptures with a developing move, aiming at h7 and the king's diagonal. White is a pawn down for quick development and open lines, which is some compensation but not enough.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Qe2.strategy: Hits the pawn on e4 at once, so Black must defend it with a developing move and White gets time to follow up. It is sound but slow: the queen stands in front of the king's bishop, and White is still a pawn down with nothing yet to show for it.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: The natural defence: the knight guards the pawn on e4, develops, and covers h5, so a queen check on that square no longer works. Black keeps the extra pawn with solid development, and White must now find a way to open lines, since quiet play only leaves Black better.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Defends the extra pawn with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. The price is a pawn on d5 that the knight already attacks and a king's knight that has not yet developed, so Black gets targets more than with the natural knight move.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece but gives the extra pawn back: nothing guards e4, and the knight takes it at once. The game is level and Black's pieces come out, yet Black has dropped the point of taking the pawn.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g4.name: Bird's Opening: Swiss Gambit
1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g4.background: The Polish theoretician Alexander Wagner named the gambit in an article of 1912, which proposed this line, and had introduced it in the Swiss correspondence game Wagner-Kostin, 1910-11; it is also known as the Wagner Gambit.
1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g4.strategy: A second pawn sacrifice: the pawn aims for g5 to drive away the knight that guards e4. If Black takes it, Nxe4 regains a pawn and the knight on g4 is attacked by the queen, so White gets active pieces. The price is a loosened kingside and a pawn still down.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Offers a second pawn with a calmer feel than the pawn thrust on the kingside: after ...exd3 the bishop recaptures with a developing move and White has open lines and a lead in development. The kingside stays intact, but White is a pawn down and must keep the initiative.

1.f4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nge2.strategy: A quiet way to add pressure on e4: the knight heads for g3 to attack the pawn a second time. Black can hold it by supporting it with a pawn and keeps the extra material, so White gets slow pressure instead of open lines.

1.f4 h6 2.Nf3.strategy: A natural developing move that makes the planned ...g5 a risk: from f3 the knight eyes g5, so the pawn would be attacked twice and defended once. White gains a useful move while Black's h-pawn has done little but weaken the kingside.

1.f4 h6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once: the h-pawn move has done nothing for Black's development, and if the planned ...g5 follows, a central pawn break leaves White ahead in development against a loosened kingside. White's pieces get a free hand.

1.f4 h6 2.d4.strategy: A solid central pawn that frees the queen and the c1-bishop's route. It makes ...g5 a mistake: White trades on g5 and wins a clean pawn, since Black's queen cannot recapture. Otherwise it is a modest, closed set-up.

1.f4 h6 2.Nf3 g5.name: Bird's Opening: Hobbs-Zilbermints Gambit
1.f4 h6 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Overextends: the pawn on g5 is attacked twice and defended once, so White simply takes it and wins a clean pawn. The open h-file gives Black nothing because the rook on h1 guards h2, and Black has weakened its own kingside for two wasted moves.

1.f4 h6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and restrains White's e-pawn, the natural stance against this opening. The extra h-pawn move costs little in this closed structure, so Black reaches a solid, level game with a compact pawn centre.

1.f4 h6 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and controls e4 and d5 from a distance. The pawn on h6 now earns its place: it keeps White's knight and bishop off g5, so Black meets the f-pawn's pressure with a flexible set-up and can still choose the pawn structure.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3.strategy: The solid reply: the knight develops and joins the f-pawn in controlling e5, which discourages Black's central breaks. White commits to no particular set-up yet, and the safer move order avoids the loosening that more ambitious second moves allow.

1.f4 Nf6 2.c4.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and controls d5, meeting the knight with a clamp there instead of a kingside build-up. It leaves e5 guarded only by the f-pawn, so Black can strike for the centre at once, and no piece is developed yet.

1.f4 Nf6 2.d4.strategy: Builds a compact centre in which the two pawns hold e5, so White can develop behind them in peace. It leaves the c1-bishop hemmed in and e4 to Black's knight, but the structure is sound and gives Black no target to hit at once.

1.f4 Nf6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchet the king's bishop and covers h4, the square White's advanced f-pawn leaves weak. It is a solid, patient set-up that aims for a safe king and pressure on the long diagonal rather than for an early central fight.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, whose long diagonal pressures the centre and the queenside, and to castle early. Black keeps the central pawns flexible and contests the long diagonal; the price is slower control of the centre.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre with a pawn, controlling e4 so that White cannot easily advance there. Black gets a solid game with a firm grip on the centre, and the game becomes a manoeuvring fight over the squares around e4 and e5.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: A flexible, solid move: it opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop and keeps the d-pawn free to choose a set-up later. It is a little passive, since it does not claim the centre at once, but it leaves Black with no weaknesses.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.b4.name: Bird's Opening: Batavo-Polish Attack
1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space and frees b2 for the bishop, aiming it down the long diagonal at Black's fianchetto. It is an ambitious, offbeat plan that commits the queenside before the centre is settled and gives Black targets for ...a5 and ...c5 breaks.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3.strategy: Answers the fianchetto in kind: the king's bishop on g2 contests the long diagonal and the king castles into safety. Both sides hold the centre from a distance, so the game stays quiet and strategic.

1.f4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop for the long diagonal, where it presses on the centre and meets Black's fianchettoed bishop. It commits less on the queenside than a pawn advance and keeps the choice of kingside set-up open.
